cases.title: A.D.M. Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla
cases.facts:
During the National Emergency declared in 1975, the Government suspended the enforcement of
fundamental rights, including the right to life and liberty under Article 21. Hundreds of political
dissidents were detained without trial under the Maintenance of Internal Security Act (MISA). The
respondents filed petitions for Habeas Corpus in various High Courts, challenging their detentions.
The State argued that during an emergency, the right to approach courts for liberty is completely
extinguished.
cases.issues:
1. Can the right to file a writ of Habeas Corpus be suspended during a National Emergency?
2. Does Article 21 remain the sole repository of the right to life and liberty?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Activist
The detainees argued that even if Article 21 is suspended, the common law and statutory rights to
liberty remain. The executive cannot act without the authority of law to deprive a person of life.
B. Respondent / State
The State argued that under Article 359, the President's order had suspended the right to move any
court. Liberty is a gift of the Constitution; if the Constitution suspends the right, no remedy exists.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: In a 4:1 majority, the Supreme Court ruled that during an Emergency, no person has any
locus standi to move a writ for personal liberty.
cases.reasoning:
The majority held that Article 21 is the 'sole repository' of the right to life and liberty. Once the
enforcement of that right is suspended by a Presidential Order, the courts are powerless to intervene,
even in cases of mala fide detention. Justice H.R. Khanna famously dissented, arguing that the right
to life existed before the Constitution and the State has no power to deprive a person of life without
the authority of law, regardless of an emergency.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. (Historical standard): Fundamental rights were seen as creations of the Constitution rather
than inherent human rights.
2. This judgment is now considered the 'darkest hour' of Indian legal history.
3. The 44th Amendment later ensured that Articles 20 and 21 can never be suspended.

cases.title: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
cases.facts:
The government impounded Maneka Gandhi's passport under the Passports Act in 'public interest'
without giving her any prior notice or a hearing. When she asked for the reasons, the government
refused to provide them. She challenged the action as a violation of her fundamental right to travel
abroad and her right to liberty under Article 21.
cases.issues:
1. Is the 'Procedure established by Law' in Article 21 required to be 'just, fair and reasonable'?
2. Does the right to travel abroad fall within the ambit of 'Personal Liberty'?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Activist
The petitioner argued that any law depriving a person of liberty must satisfy the 'Golden Triangle'
test (Articles 14, 19, and 21). A law allowing the executive to seize a passport without a hearing is
arbitrary.
B. Respondent / State
The State argued that Article 21 only requires a 'procedure' to be written in a statute. The Passports
Act provided the procedure, so the action was constitutional.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of Maneka Gandhi, fundamentally expanding the scope of
Article 21.
cases.reasoning:
The Court overruled the old A.K. Gopalan standard. It held that 'Procedure established by law' is
not merely any procedural formality, but must be 'Just, Fair and Reasonable'-essentially
incorporating the American concept of 'Substantive Due Process'. The Court ruled that fundamental
rights are not watertight compartments; they overlap. Any law affecting liberty under Art 21 must
also pass the test of non-arbitrariness under Art 14. This established the 'Principles of Natural Justice'
(hearing before action) as an inseparable part of Article 21.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. The 'Just, Fair and Reasonable' test for Article 21.
2. Right to travel abroad is a part of 'Personal Liberty'.
3. Overruling of the watertight compartment theory of fundamental rights.

cases.title: K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India
cases.facts:
The government's ' Aadhaar' scheme, which involved the collection of biometric data of all citizens,
was challenged. The central question was whether the Indian Constitution contains an implicit
fundamental 'Right to Privacy', given that it is not explicitly mentioned in Part III. The State relied on
old judgments (Kharak Singh/M.P . Sharma) to argue that privacy is not a fundamental right.
cases.issues:
1. Is the Right to Privacy a fundamental right under the Indian Constitution?
2. Does Article 21 encompass a right to bodily and data informational privacy?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Activist
Petitioners argued that liberty is meaningless without privacy. Privacy is a natural right inherent in
the dignity of a human being and is protected under Articles 14, 19, and 21.
B. Respondent / State
The State argued that the Constitution-makers deliberately omitted privacy. It claimed that privacy is
an 'elitist' concept and that for a developing nation, public welfare (Aadhaar) takes precedence over
individual privacy.
cases.judgment: Ruling: A 9-Judge Bench unanimously declared that the Right to Privacy is a Fundamental Right.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that privacy is an essential component of 'dignity', 'liberty', and 'autonomy'. It is the
'inner sanctum' of the individual. The Court ruled that although not explicitly mentioned, privacy is
the core of all fundamental rights. It protects the individual from State intrusion into their homes,
bodies, choices, and data. Any State restriction on privacy must meet a 3-fold test: (a) Legality
(backed by a law), (b) Necessity (serving a legitimate state aim), and (c) Proportionality.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Right to Privacy is a fundamental right under Article 21.
2. Privacy includes bodily integrity, personal autonomy, and informational self-determination.
3. Privacy is not a gift of the state but a natural right inherent in humans.

cases.title: Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan
cases.facts:
Bhanwari Devi, a social worker in Rajasthan, was gang-raped by local men as retaliation for her
efforts to stop child marriages. Despite the horrific crime, the criminal justice system failed to provide
her justice. A group of women's rights NGOs (Vishaka) filed a PIL in the Supreme Court highlighting
the total absence of laws to protect women from sexual harassment at the workplace.
cases.issues:
1. Can the Supreme Court frame 'guidelines' to fill a legislative vacuum in human rights?
2. Does sexual harassment at work violate the right to life and dignity under Article 21?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Activist
The petitioners argued that working women are entitled to a safe environment. Sexual harassment is
a form of gender discrimination and a violation of the right to practice any profession (Art 19(1)(g))
and the right to life with dignity (Art 21).
B. Respondent / State
The State did not oppose the need for protection but acknowledged the lack of statutory laws
governing private and public sector workplaces.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court issued the 'Vishaka Guidelines', which had the force of law until
Parliament passed the POSH Act in 2013.
cases.reasoning:
The Court invoked Article 141 (binding nature of SC judgments) and international conventions like
CEDAW. It held that sexual harassment is a clear violation of gender equality and dignity. Since no
domestic law existed, the Court exercised its power to 'frame law' by issuing mandatory guidelines.
These included the requirement to form Internal Complaints Committees (ICC), defining harassment,
and mandating employer accountability.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Right against sexual harassment is a fundamental human right.
2. Judicial legislation: Courts can fill legislative gaps to protect fundamental rights.
3. Integration of International Human Rights treaties into domestic law.

cases.title: Hussainara Khatoon v. Home Secretary, State of Bihar
cases.facts:
This was the first major 'Public Interest Litigation' (PIL) in India. A newspaper report revealed that
thousands of 'undertrial prisoners' in Bihar jails were languishing for periods longer than the
maximum sentence they would have received if convicted. Many had been forgotten by the system
for over a decade for minor offenses because they were too poor to afford bail or lawyers.
cases.issues:
1. Does the Right to Life (Article 21) include the 'Right to a Speedy Trial'?
2. Is the State obligated to provide 'Free Legal Aid' to the poor under Article 21?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Activist
The petitioner argued that the 'procedure' of keeping people in jail indefinitely without trial is
neither just nor reasonable. It is a form of state-sponsored torture against the poor.
B. Respondent / State
The State admitted the delays, citing a shortage of judges and heavy backlogs in the criminal justice
system.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ordered the immediate release of thousands of prisoners and established
the Right to a Speedy Trial.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that 'speedy trial' is an integral part of the 'just, fair and reasonable' procedure
guaranteed by Article 21. No person can be deprived of liberty through a procedure that is
heartlessly slow. The Court also ruled that the right to 'Free Legal Services' for the poor is a
mandatory constitutional obligation of the State, without which the right to a fair trial is a myth. The
Court used the PIL mechanism to monitor jail conditions.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Right to Speedy Trial is a fundamental human right under Article 21.
2. Right to Free Legal Aid is a mandatory facet of the right to life.
3. The birth of PIL in India for the protection of marginalized groups.

cases.title: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
cases.facts:
A letter was sent to the Chief Justice highlighting the alarming rise in deaths in police custody
(custodial torture). The petitioner sought guidelines to make the police accountable and ensure that
no person taken into custody is subjected to inhuman or degrading treatment.
cases.issues:
1. What safeguards are necessary to prevent custodial violence and torture?
2. Can the State be held liable to pay compensation for the violation of Article 21 by its officers?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Activist
The petitioner argued that custodial torture is a 'naked violation of human dignity'. Police stations
were becoming 'torture chambers' because there were no transparent rules for arrest.
B. Respondent / State
The State argued that existing laws (CrPC) already protected rights and that individual rogue officers
should be prosecuted, rather than the whole department.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court issued 11 mandatory guidelines (The D.K. Basu Guidelines) for arrest
and detention and established the right to compensation.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that 'Custodial Torture' is a blow to the Rule of Law. To prevent 'third-degree'
methods, the Court mandated: (1) Arrest memos, (2) Right to inform a relative, (3) Mandatory
medical checkups, and (4) Transparent records. Most importantly, the Court established the 'Public
Law Remedy'-the State is liable to pay monetary compensation to the victims or their families for
the violation of fundamental rights by police officers, regardless of any sovereign immunity.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Protection against custodial torture and inhuman treatment.
2. Mandatory transparency and documentation during arrest.
3. Sovereign Immunity is no defense against a claim for compensation for the violation of Article
21.

cases.title: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India
cases.facts:
Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC), a 150-year-old colonial law, criminalized 'carnal
intercourse against the order of nature', effectively making same-sex relations between consenting
adults a criminal offense. Members of the LGBTQ+ community challenged the law, arguing it
violated their right to equality, privacy, and dignity.
cases.issues:
1. Does the criminalization of private, consensual same-sex acts violate Articles 14, 15, 19, and 21?
2. Does 'Sex' in Article 15 include 'Sexual Orientation'?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Activist
Petitioners argued that sexual orientation is a core part of human identity. Criminalizing it forces an
entire class of citizens to live as 'second-class' citizens in constant fear, violating their dignity.
B. Respondent / State
Conservative groups argued that homosexuality is 'against the order of nature' and that the
legislature, not the court, should decide on social morality.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court struck down Section 377 to the extent it criminalized consensual acts
between adults.
cases.reasoning:
The Court ruled that 'Constitutional Morality' must prevail over 'Social Morality'. It held that sexual
orientation is an inherent part of 'Privacy' and 'Dignity' under Article 21. Discrimination based on
orientation violates the right to equality. The Court famously apologized to the LGBTQ+ community
for the historical injustice and delay in recognizing their rights. It ruled that Section 377 had a
'chilling effect' on the freedom of expression and identity of millions of Indians.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Decriminalization of consensual same-sex relations.
2. Right to Sexual Orientation is a fundamental human right.
3. The doctrine of Constitutional Morality.

cases.title: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India
cases.facts:
This followed the 2017 Privacy judgment. The Court had to decide if the Aadhaar Act itself was
constitutional. Critics argued that mandating Aadhaar for bank accounts, SIM cards, and school
admissions created a 'surveillance state' and violated the right to data privacy.
cases.issues:
1. Can the State mandate biometric identification for social welfare schemes?
2. Does the Aadhaar Act satisfy the test of 'Proportionality'?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Activist
The petitioners argued that Aadhaar was an overbroad measure that excluded the poor (due to
biometric failures) and allowed the government to track every movement of a citizen.
B. Respondent / State
The State argued that Aadhaar was essential to plug leakages in the subsidy system and ensure that
the 'right to food' and other welfare reaches the truly needy.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court upheld Aadhaar for social welfare but struck down its mandatory use by
private companies.
cases.reasoning:
Applying the 3-fold test of Privacy, the Court found that Aadhaar for welfare schemes (subsidies) had
a 'legitimate state aim'-to protect the human rights of the poor to receive benefits. It was
proportionate because it used minimal data for a massive public good. However, the Court struck
down Section 57 which allowed 'private corporations' (banks/telecoms) to use Aadhaar, as that was
not a 'necessary' or 'legitimate' state interest and posed a massive privacy risk.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Proportionality Test for privacy violations.
2. State can mandate identification for welfare, but not for private commercial services.
3. Protection of 'Digital Human Rights' against private data mining.

cases.title: National Legal Services Authority (NALSA) v. Union of India
cases.facts:
The transgender community in India lived on the extreme margins of society, denied legal
recognition of their gender identity. They were forced to identify as either 'Male' or 'Female' in all
official documents, leading to harassment and denial of basic rights to education, health, and
employment. A PIL was filed seeking legal recognition for a 'Third Gender'.
cases.issues:
1. Does the Right to Life (Article 21) include the 'Right to Gender Identity'?
2. Does discrimination against transgenders violate the equality guarantee of Article 14 and 15?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Activist
The petitioners argued that 'Self-determination of Gender' is the highest form of personal liberty.
Forcing them to adopt a binary gender they do not identify with is a violation of their dignity and
freedom of expression (Art 19).
B. Respondent / State
The State argued that legal systems were historically built on the binary and that recognizing a third
gender required complex legislative changes in marriage, succession, and criminal laws.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court recognized Transgender persons as a 'Third Gender' and affirmed their
fundamental rights.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that gender identity is not just about biological sex but about an individual's 'internal
sense of being'. Discrimination on the ground of gender identity is discrimination on the ground of
'sex' under Article 15. The Court ruled that every person has a right to choose their gender identity. It
directed the government to provide them with 'Third Gender' status in all documents and to treat
them as 'Socially and Educationally Backward Classes' (SEBC) for reservations in education and jobs.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Recognition of the 'Third Gender'.
2. Right to Gender Identity and Self-determination as a fundamental right under Article 21.
3. Mandatory affirmative action for the transgender community.

cases.title: Shafin Jahan v. Asokan K.M.
cases.facts:
Hadiya, a 24-year-old medical student, converted to Islam and married Shafin Jahan. Her father filed
a Habeas Corpus petition in the High Court, alleging she was 'brainwashed' or 'indoctrinated'. The
Kerala High Court annulled the marriage, calling it a 'sham', and handed her over to her father's
custody, essentially keeping her under house arrest. The husband appealed.
cases.issues:
1. Does a court have the power to annul a marriage between two consenting adults?
2. Does the right to life include the 'Right to Choose a Life Partner'?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Activist
The father argued it was a case of 'Love Jihad' and his daughter's consent was not free due to
psychological manipulation.
B. Respondent / State
Hadiya appeared in court and categorically stated she had converted and married of her own free
will. She argued that as an adult, the court cannot dictate her choice of religion or husband.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order, restoring the marriage and Hadiya's
freedom.
cases.reasoning:
The Court issued a powerful defense of individual autonomy. It held that the right to choose a
partner and the right to change one's religion are core components of 'Privacy' and 'Liberty' under
Article 21. A court cannot act as a 'super-parent' over consenting adults. The High Court's act of
annulling a valid marriage was a 'patriarchal' overreach that crushed the human rights of a woman.
The Court ruled that no person, including parents or the State, can interfere in the private choices of
an adult.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Right to Choose a Life Partner is a fundamental human right.
2. Right to Religion includes the right to convert.
3. Individual autonomy and the limits of the Parens Patriae doctrine.

cases.title: Joseph Shine v. Union of India
cases.facts:
Section 497 of the IPC made ' Adultery' a criminal offense. However, the law was unique: it only
punished the man who had relations with a married woman. It did not punish the woman, and more
importantly, it treated the woman as the 'property' of her husband (the crime only existed if the
husband didn't consent). A PIL was filed to strike down this discriminatory law.
cases.issues:
1. Does criminalizing adultery violate the right to equality (Art 14) and the right against gender
discrimination (Art 15)?
2. Does the law violate the privacy and dignity of women by treating them as chattel?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Activist
The petitioner argued that the law was based on Victorian-era patriarchy. It punished only men but
insulted women by assuming they have no agency or sexual autonomy independent of their
husbands.
B. Respondent / State
The State argued that adultery is a 'social wrong' that destroys the sanctity of marriage and should
remain a crime to protect the family unit.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court struck down Section 497 IPC as unconstitutional.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the law was 'archaic and paternalistic'. It treated a married woman as the
'property' of her husband. Criminalizing a private act of infidelity between adults is a violation of the
'Right to Privacy'. The Court ruled that while adultery may be a ground for divorce, it cannot be a
'crime' in a modern democracy. The law also violated Article 14 because it discriminated against men
(who were punished) and women (who were treated as incapable of consent).
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Decriminalization of Adultery.
2. Women are not the property of their husbands.
3. Sexual Autonomy is a part of the Right to Life (Article 21).

cases.title: Common Cause v. Union of India
cases.facts:
An NGO filed a PIL seeking the legal recognition of 'Living Wills'-documents where a person can
state in advance that if they fall into a permanent vegetative state (PVS), they should not be kept alive
on artificial life support. The petitioner sought the right to 'die with dignity'.
cases.issues:
1. Does the Right to Life (Article 21) include the 'Right to Die with Dignity'?
2. Is 'Passive Euthanasia' (withdrawing life support) legally permissible in India?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Activist
Petitioners argued that forcing a person to stay alive in extreme pain or as a 'living vegetable' through
machines is inhuman treatment. Dignity is the core of life, and a person should have the right to
refuse treatment.
B. Respondent / State
The State expressed concerns about potential misuse of living wills by relatives to inherit property
sooner. They argued that the state has a duty to protect all lives.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court recognized the right to Passive Euthanasia and 'Living Wills'.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the 'Right to Die with Dignity' is an inseparable part of the Right to Life under
Article 21. Life without dignity is not life. A person has the 'Right to Self-determination' regarding
their own medical treatment. The Court legalized 'Passive Euthanasia' (allowing nature to take its
course by removing machines) but strictly prohibited ' Active Euthanasia' (lethal injections). The
Court also laid down complex guidelines for executing 'Living Wills' to prevent any misuse.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Right to Die with Dignity is a fundamental human right.
2. Legal recognition of 'Passive Euthanasia'.
3. Individual autonomy over medical decisions at the end of life.

cases.title: People's Union for Civil Liberties (PUCL) v. Union of India
cases.facts:
During a period of severe drought, millions of people were on the verge of starvation, while
government granaries (FCI) were overflowing with rotting food grains. The PUCL filed a PIL arguing
that the State's failure to distribute excess food while people starved was a violation of the right to
life.
cases.issues:
1. Does the Right to Life (Article 21) include the 'Right to Food'?
2. Can the Court issue mandatory directives to the State to implement social welfare schemes?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Activist
The petitioner argued that 'Life' means more than survival. The State has a positive obligation to
ensure that no citizen dies of hunger when food is available.
B. Respondent / State
The State argued that food security is a policy and economic issue and that the 'Directive Principles'
(Art 47) are not enforceable in a court of law.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court recognized the Right to Food and converted several welfare schemes into
legal entitlements.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that Article 21 is a 'guarantee against starvation'. It issued a series of interim orders
(Continuing Mandamus) that transformed the 'Mid-Day Meal Scheme' into a mandatory right for
every school-going child. It also mandated the proper functioning of the PDS (ration shops) and
food-for-work programs. This case established that the State's duty to protect life includes providing
the basic means of sustenance.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Right to Food is a fundamental right under Article 21.
2. Conversion of non-justiciable 'Directive Principles' into enforceable 'Fundamental Rights' via
judicial interpretation.
3. The State's accountability for starvation deaths.

cases.title: Prem Shankar Shukla v. Delhi Administration
cases.facts:
A prisoner challenged the practice of the police to routinely 'handcuff' undertrial prisoners when
transporting them from jail to court. He argued that being paraded in public with handcuffs was
humiliating and unnecessary for most non-violent prisoners.
cases.issues:
1. Does the routine use of handcuffs violate the human dignity of a prisoner?
2. What are the limits of police power to use physical restraints on detainees?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Activist
The prisoner argued that handcuffs are an 'affront to human dignity'. Unless there is a proven risk of
escape or violence, the police have no right to treat an undertrial as a dangerous animal.
B. Respondent / State
The police argued that handcuffs were necessary for security and to prevent escapes in crowded
court premises.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court banned the routine use of handcuffs.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that 'Human Dignity' is the signature of our Constitution. Handcuffs should be the
last resort, not the first. To handcuff is to 'hoist the flag of the police state' over the individual. The
Court ruled that handcuffs can only be used if there is 'clear and convincing' evidence that the
prisoner is violent or has a history of escape. The police must record the reasons for handcuffing in
writing, and the Magistrate must approve them. Routine handcuffing was declared a violation of
Articles 14, 19, and 21.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Right against routine handcuffing.
2. Human Dignity is a non-negotiable part of Article 21.
3. Strict judicial oversight of police methods of restraint.

cases.title: Indian Young Lawyers Association v. State of Kerala
cases.facts:
The Sabarimala Temple in Kerala followed a long-standing custom of prohibiting women of
'menstruating age' (10-50 years) from entering the shrine, citing the 'celibate nature' of the deity, Lord
Ayyappa. A group of female lawyers challenged this custom as being discriminatory and against the
human rights of women.
cases.issues:
1. Does a religious custom prohibiting women violate the right to equality (Art 14) and freedom of
religion (Art 25)?
2. Can 'Biological Attributes' (menstruation) be used to exclude a class of citizens from public
worship?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Activist
Petitioners argued that the ban was a form of 'Untouchability' (Art 17) based on patriarchal notions of
impurity. It violated women's right to worship and their dignity.
B. Respondent / State
The temple authorities argued that the custom was an 'Essential Religious Practice' and that devotees
have a right to manage their own religious affairs (Art 26). They argued the exclusion was not about
misogyny but about the specific nature of the deity.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court (4:1 majority) struck down the ban and allowed women of all ages to
enter.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that 'Patriarchy cannot be allowed to trump Liberty'. Religious practices that treat
women as 'lesser' or 'impure' violate Constitutional Morality. The Court ruled that the right to
religion (Art 25) belongs to individuals, not just institutions, and it is subject to the guarantee of
equality. Menstruation is a natural biological process and using it to bar entry is a form of
discrimination. (Note: Justice Indu Malhotra dissented, arguing that religious sentiments should not
be judged by secular tests of logic).
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Gender equality prevails over exclusionary religious customs.
2. Biological factors cannot be used for discrimination in public spaces/temples.
3. Constitutional Morality over tradition.

cases.title: Mithu v. State of Punjab
cases.facts:
Section 303 of the IPC mandated an absolute 'Death Penalty' for any person who committed murder
while already serving a life sentence for another crime. This section left the judges with no discretion
to award a lesser sentence, unlike Section 302 where life imprisonment is an option.
cases.issues:
1. Does a 'Mandatory Death Penalty' violate the right to life and equality?
2. Can the law create a different punishment for the same crime based solely on the status of the
accused as a 'life convict'?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Activist
The petitioner argued that Section 303 was arbitrary. A person could have committed a 'mercy
killing' or acted in self-defense, but the law would still force the judge to hang them just because they
were a life convict. This violates Articles 14 and 21.
B. Respondent / State
The State argued that a life convict who kills again shows that they are 'beyond reform', and a
mandatory death sentence is necessary for deterrence in prisons.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court struck down Section 303 as unconstitutional.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that a 'mandatory' death sentence is the 'antithesis of a fair procedure'. Every accused
has a right to be heard on the question of sentence. Taking away the judge's discretion to consider
mitigating circumstances is 'savage' and 'arbitrary'. The Court also ruled that the classification of 'life
convicts' into a separate class for murder was not a rational differentia. Section 303 was declared void,
and all such murderers are now tried under Section 302.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Mandatory death penalty is unconstitutional.
2. Right to be heard on sentencing is a fundamental human right.
3. Arbitrary classifications in criminal law violate Article 14.

cases.title: Sheela Barse v. State of Maharashtra
cases.facts:
A journalist, Sheela Barse, wrote a letter to the Supreme Court after visiting the Bombay City Lock-
up, describing the horrific conditions of female prisoners. She reported that women were being
physically assaulted and abused by male police officers in the lock-up and that they had no separate
facilities or protection.
cases.issues:
1. What human rights protections are necessary for female prisoners in police custody?
2. Can the Court issue directives for 'Custodial Transparency'?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Activist
The petitioner argued that a woman in police custody is in a 'vulnerable' position. The absence of
female guards and lack of information about their rights led to systematic sexual abuse.
B. Respondent / State
The State admitted the lack of infrastructure but argued that police reforms were a slow
administrative process.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court issued mandatory directives for the protection of women in custody.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the State has a 'special duty' to ensure the safety of women and children in its
custody. It mandated that: (1) Female prisoners must be kept in separate lock-ups. (2) They must be
guarded by female police officers only. (3) Interrogations of women must be done in the presence of
female officers. (4) Arrested persons must be immediately informed of their right to legal aid. The
Court directed that these rules be displayed in every police station in local languages.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Right of women to be guarded by women in custody.
2. Custodial safety is a facet of the Right to Life.
3. Transparency in arrest procedures as a shield against abuse.

cases.title: Shakti Vahini v. Union of India
cases.facts:
NGO Shakti Vahini filed a PIL regarding the surge in 'Honor Killings' across North India. Khap
Panchayats (extra-judicial community councils) were issuing 'fatwas' or decrees against young
couples who married outside their caste or religion, often resulting in their brutal murder by family
members. The State authorities were often seen as complicit or inactive.
cases.issues:
1. Does the right to life include the human right to choose one's own partner without community
interference?
2. Can the State be held liable for failing to prevent 'private' violence against inter-caste couples?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Activist
The petitioner argued that 'Honor' has no place in a democratic society if it means killing innocent
people. The Khap Panchayats were acting as a 'parallel legal system' in violation of the Constitution.
B. Respondent / State
State governments argued that these were law and order issues and they were taking criminal action
after the crimes happened.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court condemned honor killings and issued comprehensive 'Preventive,
Remedial and Punitive' guidelines.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that 'Liberty' includes the right to 'choice'. When two adults consensually marry, no
one-parents, community, or Khaps-has the right to interfere. Choice is an individual's 'human
right' protected by Article 21. The Court ruled that 'Honor Killings' are cold-blooded murders. It
ordered the police to identify vulnerable areas, provide safe houses for runaway couples, and
mandated that any Khap Panchayat issuing such a decree be immediately prosecuted. It held the
State accountable for 'failing to protect' the lives of citizens from private non-state actors.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Right to Choice of marriage is a fundamental human right.
2. Khap Panchayats and extra-judicial decrees are illegal.
3. The State has a 'Positive Duty' to prevent honor crimes.

cases.title: Laxmi v. Union of India
cases.facts:
Laxmi, an acid attack survivor, filed a PIL highlighting the ease with which corrosive acid could be
purchased in India for a few rupees and the total lack of medical and financial support for survivors.
Acid attacks were used as a weapon to destroy the identity and dignity of women.
cases.issues:
1. Should the State regulate the sale of hazardous substances like acid to protect human rights?
2. What is the State's liability regarding the medical treatment and rehabilitation of acid attack
survivors?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Activist
The petitioner argued that an acid attack is 'worse than murder' because it leaves the victim in
permanent physical and mental agony. The State's failure to regulate acid sales was a direct cause of
these violations.
B. Respondent / State
The State argued that acid is used in various small-scale industries and households, making a total
ban difficult.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court regulated the sale of acid and mandated free medical treatment for
survivors.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the State must prioritize 'public safety' over 'commercial convenience'. It issued
mandatory rules: (1) Acid cannot be sold to anyone under 18. (2) Buyers must provide ID and state
the purpose of use. (3) All stock must be declared to the police. Regarding the victims, the Court
ruled that the State is under a 'Human Rights' obligation to provide free treatment and surgery in all
public and private hospitals and ordered a minimum compensation of Rs. 3 lakhs to be paid by the
State.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. State responsibility to regulate hazardous items to prevent human rights violations.
2. Right to free medical care for victims of heinous crimes.
3. Recognition of 'dignity' and 'bodily identity' under Article 21.

cases.title: Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation
cases.facts:
The BMC decided to forcibly evict thousands of pavement dwellers (squatters) living in slums on the
sidewalks of Mumbai. The eviction was to be done without providing any alternative housing or
even a prior notice. The dwellers, led by journalist Olga Tellis, challenged the eviction as a violation of
their right to survive.
cases.issues:
1. Does the Right to Life (Article 21) include the 'Right to Livelihood'?
2. Can a person be evicted from public land without 'Due Process'?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Activist
The dwellers argued that they lived on the streets because they worked nearby as daily wagers. If
they are evicted, they lose their jobs and thus their means of life. Therefore, the right to work is a part
of the right to life.
B. Respondent / State
The BMC argued that the pavements are for public transport and that the squatters had no 'legal
right' to occupy public property.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court recognized the Right to Livelihood but allowed the eviction subject to
procedural fairness.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark ruling: ' An equally important facet of the right to life is the right to
livelihood because no person can live without the means of living.' If the right to livelihood is not
treated as a part of the right to life, the easiest way to deprive a person of their life would be to
deprive them of their means of livelihood. However, the Court also noted that pavements are public
property. It ruled that while the State can evict squatters, it must follow 'Natural Justice'. No one can
be evicted without a 'notice' and a 'hearing'. The Court also urged the State to provide alternative
shelter to ensure the dwellers were not reduced to absolute destitution.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Right to Livelihood is a fundamental human right under Article 21.
2. Natural Justice (Right to be heard) is mandatory even for illegal squatters.
3. The State must balance public space management with the human right to survival.

cases.title: Sunil Batra v. Delhi Administration
cases.facts:
Sunil Batra, a prisoner under a death sentence, challenged the practice of keeping such prisoners in
'solitary confinement' from the moment the sentence is passed until execution. He argued that this
practice, often lasting years during appeals, was inhuman and violated his right to life and dignity.
cases.issues:
1. Can a prisoner be kept in solitary confinement solely because they are under a death sentence?
2. Do fundamental rights stop at the prison gates?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Advocate
The petitioner argued that solitary confinement is a separate, additional punishment not authorized
by the court. Prisoners are humans and are entitled to the protection of Article 21.
B. Respondent / State Authority
The prison authorities argued that Section 30(2) of the Prisons Act required death-row inmates to be
'confined in a cell apart from all other prisoners' for safety and to prevent suicide.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled that solitary confinement of death-row inmates is illegal and can
only be imposed in extreme cases.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that 'Personal Liberty' under Article 21 is not totally lost even in prison. It held that
Section 30(2) only meant a separate cell for sleeping, not a total denial of human contact. Solitary
confinement is a harsh psychological punishment that can only be imposed as a disciplinary measure
under judicial oversight. The Court famously declared that 'Fundamental Rights do not flee the
person as he enters the prison'.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Prisoners' rights are an extension of Article 21.
2. Solitary confinement cannot be used as a routine administrative measure.
3. The judiciary has the duty to oversee prison conditions through 'Writ Jurisdiction'.

cases.title: Kharak Singh v. State of U.P.
cases.facts:
Kharak Singh, a man acquitted of dacoity, was put under 'surveillance' by the police. This included
opening a 'history sheet' for him, secret picketing of his house, and 'domiciliary visits' at night where
police would wake him up to check his presence.
cases.issues:
1. Does police surveillance violate the right to freedom of movement (Art 19) and personal liberty
(Art 21)?
2. Is the right to privacy part of the right to life?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Advocate
The petitioner argued that being woken up at night and followed by police violated his human
dignity and his right to be left alone.
B. Respondent / State Authority
The State argued that surveillance was necessary for maintaining public order and preventing crime,
as per the U.P . Police Regulations.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court struck down the night-time domiciliary visits as unconstitutional.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that 'Personal Liberty' under Article 21 is a broad term including everything that goes
to make up the personal liberties of a man. Night visits were an unauthorized intrusion into a
person's home, which is his castle. While the majority at the time did not explicitly recognize a 'Right
to Privacy', the dissenting opinion of Justice Subba Rao argued that privacy is an essential ingredient
of personal liberty, a view that was finally upheld in the Puttaswamy judgment decades later.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Personal Liberty includes the right against unauthorized police intrusion into the home.
2. Executive regulations must be backed by a valid 'Law' to restrict fundamental rights.
3. Every man's house is his castle; sanctity of the home is a human right.

cases.title: Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India
cases.facts:
An NGO (Bonded Labour Liberation Front) filed a PIL highlighting the plight of thousands of
'bonded laborers' working in stone quarries in Haryana. The workers were living in sub-human
conditions, exposed to toxic dust, denied minimum wages, and kept in physical bondage to settle
petty debts.
cases.issues:
1. Is the State obligated to identify and rehabilitate bonded laborers under Article 21?
2. Can the Court act on an informal letter to protect human rights?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Advocate
The petitioner argued that forced labor (Art 23) is a denial of the right to life with dignity. The State
was complicit by failing to enforce the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act.
B. Respondent / State Authority
The State of Haryana denied the existence of bonded labor and argued that the PIL was an
interference with administrative matters and state sovereignty.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ordered the immediate release and rehabilitation of the laborers.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the Right to Life includes the right to live with basic human dignity, free from
exploitation. When a person is forced to work against their will to repay a debt, it is a form of slavery.
The Court ruled that it is the 'constitutional duty' of the State to proactively identify and free bonded
laborers. The Court used its power of 'Continuing Mandamus' to monitor the rehabilitation and
ensure the workers were given housing and food.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Right against forced labor and bondage is a non-negotiable human right.
2. The State has a 'positive obligation' to protect citizens from private exploitation.
3. PIL is a valid tool to enforce the rights of the 'voiceless' and illiterate poor.

cases.title: People's Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India
cases.facts:
During the 1982 Asian Games in Delhi, thousands of migrant workers were employed in massive
construction projects. They were paid less than the 'Minimum Wage', and deductions were made by
middlemen (jamadars). A PIL was filed alleging a violation of Article 23 (prohibition of forced labor).
cases.issues:
1. Does paying less than minimum wage amount to 'forced labor' under Article 23?
2. Can a private contract be scrutinized by the Supreme Court under Article 32?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Advocate
The petitioner argued that 'force' is not just physical force; it includes 'economic force'. If a person
works for less than a living wage out of hunger, they are forced to work.
B. Respondent / State Authority
The Government argued that the workers joined voluntarily and that the dispute was a matter of
industrial law, not fundamental rights.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled that paying less than the minimum wage is 'Forced Labour'.
cases.reasoning:
The Court gave a revolutionary interpretation to Article 23. It held that 'begar' or forced labor
includes any situation where a person is compelled to work due to 'force of circumstances' like
poverty or hunger. If a worker is not paid the statutory minimum wage, it is assumed their labor is
being 'extorted' through their vulnerability. The Court declared that Article 23 is enforceable not just
against the State but also against private contractors.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. 'Economic Force' constitutes forced labor under Article 23.
2. Minimum Wage is a fundamental human right.
3. Fundamental Rights are enforceable against private individuals in cases of exploitation.

cases.title: Francis Coralie Mullin v. The Administrator, UT of Delhi
cases.facts:
A British national was detained under the COFEPOSA (preventive detention law). She was denied
the right to have regular meetings with her family members and her lawyer. The prison rules only
allowed one meeting a month.
cases.issues:
1. Does the Right to Life (Art 21) include the right to human contact and family visits?
2. What is the definition of 'Life' in the Indian Constitution?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Advocate
The petitioner argued that detention only means restriction of movement; it does not mean the end of
all human relationships. The restrictive rules were cruel and arbitrary.
B. Respondent / State Authority
The State argued that a detenu under a security law has no right to demand the same facilities as an
ordinary citizen.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled that the Right to Life includes the right to live with 'Human
Dignity'.
cases.reasoning:
Justice Bhagwati delivered a poetic and powerful judgment. He held that 'Life' is not mere 'animal
existence'. It includes 'the right to live with human dignity and all that goes along with it, namely, the
bare necessities of life such as adequate nutrition, clothing and shelter... and also the right to carry on
such functions and activities as constitute the bare minimum expression of the human-self.' Denying
a prisoner the right to see their family and lawyer is a violation of this dignity.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Right to Life = Right to Human Dignity.
2. Prisoners have the right to meet their family and legal counsel.
3. Any restriction on liberty must be minimal and reasonable.

cases.title: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India
cases.facts:
A PIL highlighted the employment of thousands of children in the hazardous match and firecracker
factories of Sivakasi. The working environment was lethal, and children were denied their right to
education and a healthy childhood.
cases.issues:
1. Does the employment of children in hazardous industries violate Article 24?
2. How should the Court compensate children for the loss of their childhood?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Advocate
The petitioner argued that child labor is a crime against humanity. The State was violating Article 21
and 24 by allowing children to work with chemicals.
B. Respondent / State Authority
The manufacturers argued that child labor was a 'harsh reality' of poverty and that a sudden ban
would starve the families.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court banned child labor in hazardous tasks and ordered the creation of a
rehabilitation fund.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that 'poverty is no excuse' for the violation of the fundamental rights of children. It
ordered that for every child employed in a hazardous job, the employer must pay Rs. 20,000 into a
'Child Labour Rehabilitation Welfare Fund'. It also directed the State to provide an adult member of
the child's family with a job. The Court emphasized that education is the only long-term solution to
end this human rights violation.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Absolute prohibition of child labor in hazardous industries (Art 24).
2. Compulsory and free education as a human right.
3. Creation of specific welfare funds for the victims of human rights abuses.

cases.title: Bodhisattwa Gautam v. Subhra Chakraborty
cases.facts:
A college lecturer deceived a woman into a false marriage, impregnated her, and then forced her to
undergo an abortion. He then abandoned her. She filed a criminal complaint and sought
compensation for the violation of her dignity and right to life.
cases.issues:
1. Can the Supreme Court award compensation for 'Rape' or sexual deception under Article 32?
2. Does sexual violence constitute a violation of Article 21?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Advocate
The petitioner argued that rape is a crime against the basic human rights of a woman. It is an
'ultimate violation of dignity' that warrants immediate constitutional relief.
B. Respondent / State Authority
The accused argued that the matter was a private criminal case and compensation can only be
awarded by a criminal court after conviction.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ordered the accused to pay 'interim compensation' even before the trial
concluded.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that 'Rape' is not just an offense under the IPC; it is a violation of the fundamental
right to life and dignity under Article 21. It is a 'humiliation of the human soul'. The Court ruled that
it has the power to award interim maintenance and compensation to rape victims in a writ petition to
ensure they are not reduced to destitution during a long trial. This case recognized women's 'bodily
integrity' as a core human right.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Rape is a violation of the fundamental Right to Life.
2. Power of the Supreme Court to award interim compensation for human rights atrocities.
3. Bodily integrity and sexual autonomy are non-negotiable facets of dignity.

cases.title: Chairman, Railway Board v. Chandrim Das
cases.facts:
A Bangladeshi national was gang-raped by railway employees in a station's guest house in Kolkata.
Chandrim Das, an advocate, filed a PIL in the High Court seeking compensation for the victim. The
State argued that the victim was a foreigner and therefore not entitled to fundamental rights under
the Indian Constitution.
cases.issues:
1. Are fundamental rights (especially Article 21) available to non-citizens/foreigners in India?
2. Is the State vicariously liable for human rights violations by its employees against a tourist?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Advocate
The petitioner argued that Article 21 uses the word 'Person', not 'Citizen'. Therefore, every human
being on Indian soil is entitled to the right to life and dignity.
B. Respondent / State Authority
The State argued that its liability only extends to citizens and that the rape was a private act of the
employees for which the State cannot be held responsible.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court upheld the compensation, ruling that foreigners enjoy Article 21.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the 'Right to Life' is a universal human right. The Indian Constitution protects
the life and liberty of any person, regardless of their nationality. Rape is a violation of international
human rights norms (Universal Declaration of Human Rights). The Court ruled that since the crime
happened on State property (Railway guest house) due to the negligence of State supervisors, the
State is vicariously liable to pay compensation to the foreign victim.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Article 21 is applicable to all 'Persons' (Citizens and Foreigners alike).
2. Sexual violence is an international human right violation.
3. The State is accountable for the safety of all people within its borders.

cases.title: National Human Rights Commission v. State of Arunachal Pradesh
cases.facts:
Chakma refugees, who had fled from Bangladesh (formerly East Pakistan), were settled in Arunachal
Pradesh. The local population and powerful student unions threatened to forcibly evict them from
the state. The NHRC filed a PIL to protect the lives and properties of the Chakmas.
cases.issues:
1. Does the State have an obligation to protect 'Refugees' from private violence?
2. Can refugees be forcibly deported or evicted without due process?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Advocate
The NHRC argued that once the State settles a group, it has a 'fiduciary duty' to protect their lives.
The threat of mass eviction by mobs was a failure of the state to maintain the rule of law.
B. Respondent / State Authority
The State Government argued that the Chakmas were 'outsiders' threatening the local culture and
economy and that it could not go against the popular will of its citizens.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ordered the State to provide absolute protection to the refugees.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the 'Right to Life' (Article 21) does not distinguish between a citizen and a
refugee. No person can be deprived of their life or liberty except by 'procedure established by law'.
Forced eviction by a mob is not a procedure. The Court ruled that the State has a 'positive duty' to
protect everyone within its territory from violence. It ordered the Arunachal government to deploy
security forces and ensure the Chakmas were not harmed or evicted until their citizenship
applications were processed by the Centre.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Protection of Article 21 extends to refugees and stateless persons.
2. The State must protect individuals from 'Private/Mob Violence'.
3. The principle of 'Non-refoulement' (protection against forced deportation).

cases.title: Gaurav Jain v. Union of India
cases.facts:
A PIL highlighted the pathetic condition of children of sex workers living in red-light areas. These
children were exposed to sexual abuse, crime, and stigma, and were often denied admission to
regular schools. The petitioner sought the creation of separate 'homes' and schools for these children.
cases.issues:
1. Does the human right to dignity include the right of children of marginalized mothers to be
'integrated' into mainstream society?
2. Does segregation of children based on their parent's profession violate Article 14?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Advocate
The petitioner argued that these children were 'lost' to society. Segregated schools were necessary for
their special needs and protection.
B. Respondent / State Authority
The State argued that it was trying to provide welfare but could not force regular schools to accept
these children if other parents objected.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court rejected 'segregation' and ordered 'integration'.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that children are not the 'property' of their mothers and should not suffer for their
mother's profession. Segregating them into separate schools would 'stigmatize' them for life and
violate their right to equality. The Court held that human rights are about 'Dignity and Equality'. It
directed the government to ensure these children are admitted to regular schools and provided with
hostels. The Court ruled that the goal of the law must be the complete 'social integration' of
marginalized children into the national mainstream.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Segregation of marginalized children violates Article 14 and 21.
2. Human rights include the right to 'Social Integration'.
3. The State has a 'Parens Patriae' duty towards vulnerable children.

cases.title: Laxmi Kant Pandey v. Union of India
cases.facts:
A PIL was filed regarding the lack of regulation in 'inter-country adoptions'. There were reports that
Indian children were being 'sold' to foreigners, subjected to abuse abroad, or used as domestic slaves
because there was no monitoring system.
cases.issues:
1. What human rights safeguards are necessary to protect children in international adoptions?
2. Does the 'Right to a Family' constitute a human right for an abandoned child?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Advocate
The petitioner argued that without strict rules, inter-country adoption was becoming a form of
'human trafficking'. Children's safety must be guaranteed before they leave the country.
B. Respondent / State Authority
Adoption agencies argued that foreign adoptions provided a better life for children who would
otherwise rot in poorly funded Indian orphanages.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court laid down comprehensive guidelines for domestic and international
adoptions.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that every child has a right to 'love and affection' and a stable family environment.
While inter-country adoption is a valid way to give a child a home, it must be the 'last resort' after
domestic options are exhausted. The Court mandated that only 'recognized' agencies can handle
adoptions, and that the 'child's best interest' is the supreme consideration. It directed the creation of
'Central Adoption Resource Authority' (CARA) to monitor every single case to prevent trafficking.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. The 'Best Interest of the Child' is the paramount human rights standard.
2. Right to a Family is a facet of the right to life.
3. Mandatory State regulation of sensitive human processes to prevent trafficking.

cases.title: Bachchan Singh v. State of Punjab
cases.facts:
The constitutional validity of the 'Death Penalty' (Section 302 IPC) was challenged. The petitioner
argued that hanging a human being is 'cruel and unusual punishment' and violates the fundamental
right to life under Article 21.
cases.issues:
1. Is the Death Penalty per se unconstitutional under the Indian Constitution?
2. What is the human rights threshold for taking a human life by the State?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Advocate
The petitioner argued that human life is sacred. The State cannot claim the 'right to kill'. Life
imprisonment is a sufficient and more humane deterrent.
B. Respondent / State Authority
The State argued that the death penalty is a 'reasonable restriction' for the most heinous crimes to
protect society and maintain public order.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court upheld the death penalty but limited it to the 'Rarest of Rare' cases.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the Right to Life is not absolute; it can be taken away by a 'procedure established
by law'. However, in a civilized society, the death penalty must be the 'exception'. The Court
established the 'Rarest of Rare' doctrine: death should only be awarded when the alternative of life
imprisonment is unquestionably foreclosed. The Court mandated that judges must look at both the
'aggravating circumstances' of the crime AND the 'mitigating circumstances' of the criminal (age,
reformability) before choosing death.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Death Penalty is constitutional but restricted to the 'Rarest of Rare' cases.
2. Requirement of 'Special Reasons' in writing for a death sentence.
3. Recognition of the 'Human Dignity' of even the worst criminals.

cases.title: Shatrughan Chauhan v. Union of India
cases.facts:
Several death-row convicts whose mercy petitions had been rejected by the President after 'undue
delay' (some lasting over 10 years) filed a petition. They argued that the extreme delay in deciding
their fate caused them 'excruciating mental agony' and that their death sentences should be
commuted to life imprisonment.
cases.issues:
1. Does 'Inordinate Delay' by the Executive in deciding a mercy petition violate Article 21?
2. Can a death sentence be commuted solely on the ground of delay?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Advocate
The petitioners argued that keeping a person in the 'shadow of death' for a decade is a form of 'State
Torture'. It is inhuman and degrading treatment.
B. Respondent / State Authority
The Government argued that the President's power of mercy is 'sovereign' and cannot be questioned
by courts. Delay is due to the complexity of the cases.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court commuted the death sentences to life imprisonment due to the delay.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the 'Right to Life' includes the right to a 'Speedy Disposal' of even a mercy
petition. While the President has the power to reject mercy, the State has no right to keep a convict in
legal limbo for years. Such delay creates an 'additional' punishment not sanctioned by law. The Court
ruled that an 'inordinate, unexplained and systemic delay' is a ground for commutation. It also
banned the practice of 'solitary confinement' for death-row inmates and mandated a 14-day gap
between the rejection of mercy and execution.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Undue delay in deciding mercy petitions is a violation of Article 21.
2. Right against 'State-induced mental torture'.
3. Judicial review of the 'exercise' of the President's mercy power.

cases.title: Selvi v. State of Karnataka
cases.facts:
The police were using scientific techniques like 'Narco-analysis' (truth serum), 'Polygraph' (lie
detector), and 'Brain Electrical Activation Profile' (BEAP) on accused persons without their consent.
The petitioners challenged these tests as a violation of their right against self-incrimination and their
right to privacy.
cases.issues:
1. Do 'invasive' psychiatric tests violate the right against self-incrimination (Art 20(3))?
2. Does the right to life (Art 21) include 'Mental Privacy'?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Advocate
The petitioners argued that the mind is the 'ultimate sanctuary'. Forcing someone to reveal thoughts
through chemicals or machines is 'mental torture' and violates their right to remain silent.
B. Respondent / State Authority
The State argued that these tests were 'non-invasive' (no physical pain) and were essential for modern
criminal investigation to catch terrorists and serial killers.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court banned the non-consensual use of Narco, Polygraph, and Brain
Mapping.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark ruling on 'Mental Autonomy'. It held that Article 20(3) protects an
individual from being 'compelled to be a witness against himself'. This protection extends to 'mental'
testimonies. Forcing someone to undergo narco-analysis is an 'intrusion into the mental privacy' of a
person. The Court ruled that even if there is no physical pain, the 'psychological compulsion' used to
extract data is unconstitutional. These tests can only be done with the 'informed consent' of the
person and the results cannot be used as evidence in court.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Right to Mental Privacy is a fundamental human right.
2. Protection against 'self-incrimination' includes mental/psychological data.
3. Prohibition of 'Scientific Torture' in investigations.

cases.title: Aruna Ramchandra Shanbaug v. Union of India
cases.facts:
Aruna Shanbaug, a nurse, was brutally raped in 1973 and left in a 'Permanent Vegetative State' (PVS)
for 37 years. She was kept alive by the hospital staff at KEM Hospital through a feeding tube. A friend
(Pinki Virani) filed a petition seeking the right to stop the feeding so Aruna could die in peace.
cases.issues:
1. Does the Right to Life include the 'Right to Die'?
2. Is 'Passive Euthanasia' (withdrawing life support) legally valid for a person who cannot give
consent?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Advocate
The petitioner argued that Aruna was 'not living'-she was just an 'object' kept alive by machines.
Forcing her to continue this 'vegetative' existence was a violation of her dignity.
B. Respondent / State Authority
The nurses at KEM hospital (the real caregivers) argued that Aruna was their 'family'. She could
respond to music and food. They were willing to care for her until her natural death.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court legalized 'Passive Euthanasia' in India but refused to allow it for Aruna.
cases.reasoning:
The Court drew a vital distinction. It held that ' Active Euthanasia' (killing) is illegal. However,
'Passive Euthanasia' (letting nature take its course) is legally permissible under strict judicial
supervision. Since Aruna could not give her own consent, the Court applied the 'Best Interest Test'. It
ruled that the KEM nurses, who had cared for her for decades, were her 'next friend'-not the
petitioner. Since the nurses wanted her to live, the feeding tube remained. Aruna died naturally four
years later.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Passive Euthanasia is legally permissible under Article 21.
2. 'Right to Die with Dignity' is recognized.
3. The 'High Court' must approve all cases of withdrawing life support.

cases.title: M.C. Mehta v. State of Tamil Nadu
cases.facts:
This was an earlier iteration of the Sivakasi case. The Court found that children were being
transported in rickety buses at 3:00 AM to work in cracker factories. The factories had no ventilation
and frequent explosions killed children.
cases.issues:
1. Can the Court impose a 'Positive Duty' on the State to ensure child safety in private sectors?
2. What are the 'human rights' duties of industries dealing with explosives?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Advocate
The petitioner argued that the State was 'turning a blind eye' to mass child exploitation in exchange
for industrial taxes.
B. Respondent / State Authority
The State Government promised reforms but argued that child labor was deep-rooted in the local
economy.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court issued immediate orders banning child transport at night and
mandating factory inspections.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the State is the 'ultimate guardian' (Parens Patriae) of children. If private
industries exploit children, the State is legally responsible for their failure to monitor. The Court
ordered that no child could be employed in the manufacture of firecrackers (a hazardous process). It
also ordered that children must be provided with 'nutritious food' and 'recreational facilities' in the
non-hazardous sectors of the factories as an interim measure until they could be integrated into
schools.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. State's vicarious responsibility for private sector human rights abuses.
2. The 'Best Interest of the Child' overrides the commercial freedom of the industry.
3. Immediate judicial intervention in 'life-threatening' child labor.

cases.title: Jitendra Singh v. State of U.P.
cases.facts:
The Government of Uttar Pradesh attempted to allot 'village common lands' (including community
ponds and grazing grounds) to private industrial houses. They argued that industrialization would
create jobs and that the 'wasteland' was not being used.
cases.issues:
1. Can the State alienate community resources held in public trust for private profit?
2. Does the human right to a 'Rural Environment' protect village commons?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Advocate
The villagers argued that common lands are the 'life-blood' of the rural poor. These lands provide
fodder for cattle and maintain the local ecosystem. Allotting them to industries violates their right to
life.
B. Respondent / State Authority
The State argued that under the 'Doctrine of Eminent Domain', it has the absolute right to acquire
and allot any land for the 'public purpose' of industrial development.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court struck down the allotments, protecting the village commons.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that 'Development' cannot be an excuse to rob the poor of their communal survival
assets. Village common lands (Ponds, Grazing lands) are held by the State in 'Public Trust' for the
villagers. These lands are essential for the 'ecological and economic' survival of the rural community.
The State cannot transfer these lands to private corporations. The Court ordered the restoration of the
common lands and the removal of all industrial encroachments.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Public Trust Doctrine protects community resources from private commercialization.
2. Right to Life includes the right to 'Communal Assets'.
3. 'Development' must be socially and ecologically inclusive.

cases.title: Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum
cases.facts:
Shah Bano, a 62-year-old Muslim woman, was divorced by her husband via 'Triple Talaq'. She was
left without any means of survival. She filed for maintenance under Section 125 of the CrPC (a
secular criminal law). The husband argued that under Muslim Personal Law, he only had to pay
maintenance for three months (the Iddat period).
cases.issues:
1. Do secular human rights laws (like CrPC 125) override religious personal laws?
2. Does the right to life include the right of a divorced woman to be 'protected from destitution'?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Advocate
The petitioner argued that Section 125 is a 'humane' law meant to prevent vagrancy. A woman's right
to survive does not change with her religion.
B. Respondent / State Authority
The husband and religious boards argued that the Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with 'Shariat'
(divine law), and that Section 125 was inapplicable to Muslims.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of Shah Bano, upholding her right to lifelong maintenance.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark ruling for the human rights of women. It held that Section 125 CrPC
is a secular, remedial law designed to fulfill the constitutional goal of social justice. Its purpose is to
prevent a woman from being thrown onto the streets to die of hunger. This 'right to maintenance' is a
facet of the Right to Life (Art 21). The Court ruled that where there is a conflict between a religious
law that leads to destitution and a secular law that provides survival, the secular law must prevail to
protect human rights.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Human Rights and Social Justice override discriminatory personal law interpretations.
2. Right to Maintenance is a fundamental part of the Right to Life.
3. The law must protect women from 'economic death' after divorce.

cases.title: National Confederation of Bank Officers v. Union of India
cases.facts:
A bank rule stated that if a female employee married, she would be 'automatically' terminated from
her job. The rule did not apply to male employees. The Confederation challenged this as a gross
violation of human rights and equality.
cases.issues:
1. Is a 'Marriage Bar' in employment a violation of the right against gender discrimination (Art
15)?
2. Does the right to work include the 'Right to Family Life'?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Advocate
The petitioner argued that marriage is a fundamental human choice. Forcing a woman to choose
between her job and her husband is 'barbaric' and violates Article 14, 15, and 21.
B. Respondent / State Authority
The Bank argued that marriage leads to 'domestic distractions' and 'maternity leaves', which affect
the efficiency of a commercial organization.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court struck down the rule as 'unconstitutional' and 'sexist'.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the rule was based on the 'Victorian' notion that a woman's primary place is in
the home. This is an insult to the 'Dignity of Women'. Discrimination based on a woman's marital
status is a form of gender discrimination prohibited by Article 15. The right to marry and have a
family is a basic human right. Any employment rule that penalizes a woman for exercising this right
is arbitrary, unreasonable, and void.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. 'Marriage Bars' in employment are illegal and unconstitutional.
2. Gender equality is a core human right in the workplace.
3. The State/Employers cannot interfere in the private 'reproductive' and 'marital' choices of
employees.

cases.title: Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India
cases.facts:
In a follow-up to the bonded labor case, the petitioner highlighted that the freed laborers were now
suffering from 'Silicosis' and 'Tuberculosis' due to the lack of dust-control measures in the quarries.
The workers were literally 'breathing stone' and dying in their 30s.
cases.issues:
1. Does the Right to Life include the right to 'Safe Working Conditions'?
2. Is the State liable for the 'Slow Death' of workers in hazardous industries?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Advocate
The NGO argued that 'Freedom from Bondage' is useless if the worker dies of disease a year later.
The 'Right to Health' is a prerequisite for the 'Right to Life'.
B. Respondent / State Authority
The quarry owners argued that dust is an 'inherent' part of mining and they could not afford
expensive air filtration systems.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ordered the mandatory provision of protective gear and medical
facilities, enforcing the 'Right to Health'.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that 'Right to Life' under Article 21 would be a 'dead letter' if it did not include the
right to health. The State cannot allow its citizens to be 'slowly poisoned' in exchange for mining
royalties. The Court directed the Government to: (1) Provide free medical checkups and treatment for
Silicosis. (2) Force owners to provide water sprinklers and masks. (3) Pay compensation for every
death caused by occupational disease. This case established 'Occupational Health' as a fundamental
human right in India.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Right to Occupational Health is a fundamental human right under Article 21.
2. The State has a duty to regulate 'Health Standards' in hazardous industries.
3. Economic profitability cannot be prioritized over the lives of the workers.

cases.title: People's Union for Civil Liberties (PUCL) v. Union of India
cases.facts:
A PIL was filed challenging the validity of Section 33B of the Representation of the People Act, which
attempted to nullify a previous Supreme Court directive. The previous directive required candidates
contesting elections to disclose their criminal antecedents, educational qualifications, and assets. The
government argued that voters have no right to know such personal details.
cases.issues:
1. Do voters have a fundamental right to information about political candidates?
2. Is the 'Right to Vote' a part of the freedom of expression under Article 19(1)(a)?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Advocate
The petitioner argued that democracy requires an informed electorate. Without knowing a
candidate's record, the 'Right to Vote' is a hollow exercise, violating the freedom of expression.
B. Respondent / State Authority
The State argued that candidate disclosure is a matter of legislative policy, not a fundamental right,
and that privacy of the candidate must be protected.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court struck down Section 33B and upheld the voters' Right to Know.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the 'Right to Know' is a subset of the freedom of speech and expression (Art 19(1)
(a)). In a democracy, the little man-the voter-has a right to know the background of those who
seek to govern him. Disclosure of criminal history, assets, and education is a 'reasonable' requirement
to ensure the purity of the electoral process. The right to vote is not just a statutory right but a
fundamental human right of political expression.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Right to Information is a fundamental right under Article 19(1)(a).
2. Transparency in elections is essential for the survival of human rights in a democracy.
3. The privacy of public figures is subordinate to the public's right to an informed choice.

cases.title: Kishore Singh v. State of Rajasthan
cases.facts:
A prisoner was subjected to 'solitary confinement' and 'iron fetters' (bar fetters) inside the jail as a
disciplinary measure. He challenged these practices as medieval and cruel, violating the standards of
a civilized society.
cases.issues:
1. Does the use of bar fetters and prolonged solitary confinement violate Article 21?
2. What is the judicial standard for 'cruel and unusual punishment' in prisons?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Advocate
The petitioner argued that physical restraints and total isolation destroy the human psyche and are
forms of torture, which the Constitution prohibits even for convicts.
B. Respondent / State Authority
The prison authorities argued that these measures were necessary to maintain discipline among
'hardened' criminals and were permitted by the Prisons Act.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court condemned the use of fetters and restricted solitary confinement.
cases.reasoning:
The Court, led by Justice Krishna Iyer, held that 'Human Dignity' is the bedrock of the Constitution.
Fetters are an insult to the human person and can only be used in rare cases where there is a clear
danger of escape or violence. Solitary confinement is a 'soul-killing' punishment. The Court ruled
that prison reforms must transition from a 'retributive' to a 'rehabilitative' model. No prisoner should
be treated as a sub-human beast.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Right against cruel, inhuman, or degrading punishment.
2. Prison discipline must comply with the 'Dignity of the Individual' (Preamble).
3. Use of physical fetters requires prior judicial approval.

cases.title: Gautam Navlakha v. NIA
cases.facts:
A prominent civil rights activist was arrested under the UAP A (anti-terror law). During the litigation
over his bail, the question arose whether 'House Arrest' can be considered a valid form of 'judicial
custody' and whether it can be used in cases involving serious offenses.
cases.issues:
1. Does the power to grant 'custody' include the power to order 'House Arrest'?
2. Is House Arrest a more humane alternative to traditional prison detention under Article 21?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Advocate
The petitioner argued that given his age and health, House Arrest was a reasonable alternative that
balanced national security with his right to life.
B. Respondent / State Authority
The NIA argued that House Arrest is not explicitly mentioned in the CrPC and that it is insufficient
for preventing a high-risk individual from communicating with associates.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court recognized 'House Arrest' as a legitimate form of judicial custody.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the judiciary has the power under Section 167 of the CrPC to order 'House
Arrest' in appropriate cases. It recognized that traditional prisons are overcrowded and often violate
human rights. For older individuals or those with health issues, House Arrest provides a balance
between 'liberty' and 'custody'. This case introduced a new, less restrictive form of detention into
Indian human rights jurisprudence.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. House Arrest is a valid form of judicial custody.
2. Courts must consider the age and health of the detainee when deciding the mode of custody.
3. Evolution of 'detention' to minimize the loss of human dignity.

cases.title: Murugan v. State of Tamil Nadu
cases.facts:
A.G. Perarivalan, a convict in the Rajiv Gandhi assassination case, had spent over 31 years in prison.
His mercy petition had been pending for years, and the Governor had refused to decide on it. He
sought release based on the extreme duration of his incarceration and the State Cabinet's
recommendation for his pardon.
cases.issues:
1. Can the Governor sit on a mercy petition indefinitely?
2. Does Article 21 provide a right to be released if the executive fails to exercise its pardon power
timely?
cases.arguments:
A. Petitioner / Human Rights Advocate
The petitioner argued that 31 years was far beyond the normal life sentence. The refusal of the
Governor to act on the Cabinet's advice was unconstitutional and violated his right to liberty.
B. Respondent / State Authority
The Union argued that in cases involving national security, the President, not the Governor, had the
